answer: Shared-secret pigment tagging. Each agent is issued a unique, traceable marker pigment mixed into any artifact it produces; the registry checks pigment provenance before accepting outputs. Duplicating an identity forces the attacker to replicate distinct pigments across all clones, and any reuse or mismatch reveals the split. Karst-like porous storage of pigment histories makes forgery costly since old records must be consistently rewritten. The garden of registered artifacts grows with each clone attempt, raising the per-identity replication cost.
